Jake didn’t wait for a better moment. He planted and drove a hard kick into Wesker’s knee from the side. It was mechanical and ugly and exactly what the situation required. The joint buckled, the weight went out from under him. He went down. Hard. He hit the tile on an elbow and tried to roll, already turning it into a strike even as every nerve protested the ask. They were throwing themselves against him before momentum could return. Nea was on him in a blink, tangling his legs and trying to avoid the knife, locking one knee against a shin while she grabbed for the other ankle. Wesker’s heel connected once with her ribs; she lost air and came right back on the exhale. Dwight threw his full frame across Wesker’s shoulder, grappling his arm and smashing his wrist against the floor until the knife clattered away. Wesker howled. The cuff flared red, sparks running in waves down his spine, nearly bucking Dwight off from the angle he flailed at. Jake slid across the floor from the other side, throwing himself at the other leg and hip, catching a half kick across his flank before he managed to dig his hand against the nerves of the knee and pin it down. The cuff read multiple contact points and made a decision. A held charge gathered without warning, pushed through bone with the precision of something that had mapped him long ago. Everything in his arm clenched at once. Every old burn remembered. Gabriel launched himself across the final gap, throwing his weight on the cuff arm. He braced one knee against the crook of the elbow and set the other near the base of Wesker’s skull, shoving his head away from the fight as far as he could to steal leverage. The writhing under him was barely held in place by the joined effects of the team, desperately holding on for dear life. If he got loose, they wouldn’t get another chance this time around. This was the closest they have gotten to date. It had to work. The stretch against the shoulder threatened to dislodge the joint from its socket, his head forced against the far shoulder making it harder to catch his breath than it already was. Hands were everywhere, digging into skin and nerves already far too raw. Wesker fought for air and found barely enough. He fought for a thought and found only panic. The sound he made was reduced to a whining yell, thin at the edges with a rasp that belonged to a throat gone raw from shouting and chemical burns. Every instinct he owned screamed at him to get out from under them — twist, buck, break something, leave someone on the floor — but the body he’d trained for years didn’t answer in time. Every failed attempt at movement, every touch against the cuff only brought more retaliation. And they wouldn’t stop touching it. Gabriel ran his hand over the band in rapid sweeps, wincing slightly at the feverish heat coming off it. He tried to rotate it, looking for anything that could be seen as a weak spot or gap, but it refused to move. Trying to force it to rotate freely only increased the bucking the group was barely holding down as it was. Even injured and clearly exhausted, the man was insanely strong. One slip and the lot of them would be thrown clear in no time. He pried along the outer edges of the cuff, probing the line where metal met skin and finding nothing. Not even the faintest trace of a gap. Only angry red burns that snaked up the arm and into the sleeve, and a deep concerning line of dark veins spidering alongside them. It was fused flush somehow; clearly it hadn’t been slipped over the hand, but it had to have been attached somehow. He swept his thumb across the surface of the metal and felt the faintest texture. There. The line was no thicker than a hair, but it was there. “Dwight,” Gabriel reached a hand back, gesturing. “His knife. Can you reach it? Pass it over. I think I can wedge this open.” Dwight snaked his free leg under the nearby cart where the combat knife had slid away, catching the blade with the edge of his shoe and flicking it closer. Sparing a second to shift his leverage slightly, he snatched it up off the floor, flipped the handle, and slammed it into Gabriel’s waiting palm. “Don’t,” Wesker managed, the word a frayed thread torn off an old spool. It came out on a breath and the back half of the syllable dissolved into a clench, carried entirely by the memory of the first time he tried the exact thing he realized the survivors were doing. “Wait—DON’T—” The first drive of the blade into the seam unlocked something violent and cold. The cuff’s internals fired a full escalation in a single greedy swallow, flooding the circuit into the bones it was anchored to. For a second the world narrowed to a point just below Wesker’s wrist and then inverted. His whole body seized, his back coming off the floor like a drawn bow. His hands clawed without purchase. The cuff screamed through him, and he matched it — his own reply a rupture, torn from the very base of his spine. Every system overloaded. Every nerve ignited. His heart convulsed brutally, forgetting natural pace or function, as thought and sensation and function was torn free. Gabriel’s jaw clenched, knuckles white on the knife, and he pushed.
